'''Kate Adebola Okikiolu''' (born 1965) is a British [[mathematician]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Katherine Okikiolu - Mathematicians of the African Diaspora|url=http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/PEEPS/okikiolu_katherine.html|access-date=2020-06-10|website=www.math.buffalo.edu}}</ref> She is known for her work with [[elliptic operator|elliptic differential operators]] as well as her work with inner-city children.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Katherine Okikiolu - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Okikiolu_Katherine/ |access-date=2022-08-10 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Okikiolu was born in 1965 in [[England]]. Her father was George Olatokunbo Okikiolu, a renowned [[Nigeria]]n mathematician<ref>{{Cite web |title=Katherine Okikiolu - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Okikiolu_Katherine/ |access-date=2022-08-11 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref> and the most published black mathematician on record.<ref name="cat">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wgiTQUcE21UC&q=Kate+Okikiolu+Mathematician&pg=PA26|title=African Doctorates in Mathematics|publisher=African Mathematical Union. Commission on the History of Mathematics in Africa|isbn=9781430318675|author=Paulus Gerdes|author-link=Paulus Gerdes|year=2007|page=26}}</ref> Her [[British people|British]] mother was a high school mathematics teacher. Okikiolu received a B.A. in mathematics from [[Cambridge University]] in 1987. In 1991 she earned her Ph.D. in mathematics from the [[University of California at Los Angeles]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Katherine Okikiolu - Mathematicians of the African Diaspora |url=http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/PEEPS/okikiolu_katherine.html |access-date=2022-08-11 |website=www.math.buffalo.edu}}</ref> for her thesis ''The Analogue of the Strong Szego Limit Theorem on the Torus and the 3-Sphere''.<ref name=cat/><ref name=Spangenburg>{{cite book|last=Spangenburg|first=Ray|title=African Americans in science, math, and invention|url=https://archive.org/details/africanamericans0000span|url-access=registration|year=2003|publisher=Facts on File|location=New York, NY|isbn=0816048061|author2=Moser, Kit}}</ref><ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=40116}}</ref>

==Career==
Based on her PhD work, Okikiolu resolved a conjecture of [[Peter Jones (mathematician)|Peter Wilcox Jones]] concerning a continuous version of the [[travelling salesman problem]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Williams |first=Scott W. |date=2008 |title=Black Women in Mathematics |url=http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/PEEPS/okikiolu_katherine.html |access-date=11 August 2022}}</ref>   in her paper ''Characterization of subsets of rectifiable curves in'' {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>.}}<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Okikiolu |first1=Kathleen |title=Characterization of subsets of rectifiable curves in {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} |journal=J. London Math. Soc. |date=1992 |volume=46 |issue=2 |pages=336–348 |doi=10.1112/jlms/s2-46.2.336 |url=http://internetanalysisseminar.gatech.edu/sites/default/files/Okikiolu(1992).pdf |accessdate=20 June 2020 |archive-date=21 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200621183415/http://internetanalysisseminar.gatech.edu/sites/default/files/Okikiolu(1992).pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>
Okikiolu was an instructor and later assistant professor at [[Princeton University]] from 1993 to 1995. She then worked as a visiting assistant professor at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] and joined the faculty at the [[University of California at San Diego]] in 1995.<ref name="Spangenburg" /> In 2011 she joined the Mathematics Department at [[Johns Hopkins University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Meet Katherine Okikiolu |url=https://stemettes.org/zine/articles/meet-katherine-okikiolu/ |access-date=2022-08-11 |website=The Stemettes Zine |language=en-GB}}</ref>

She was an invited speaker at the 1996 meeting of the [[Association of Women in Mathematics]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Women and Minorities in Mathematics |url=https://cs.appstate.edu/~sjg/ncctm/ncctmcolumnfinal.html |access-date=2022-08-11 |website=cs.appstate.edu |archive-date=2022-10-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221020115744/https://cs.appstate.edu/~sjg/ncctm/ncctmcolumnfinal.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> She also delivered the Claytor-Woodard lecture at the 2002 meeting of the [[National Association of Mathematicians]], an organization for African-American mathematicians.<ref name=Spangenburg/>

==Honors and awards==
In 1997, Okikiolu won a [[Sloan Fellowship|Sloan Research Fellowship]],<ref>{{citation|url=https://sloan.org/past-fellows|title=Past Fellows|publisher=Sloan Foundation|accessdate=2019-09-09|archive-date=2018-03-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180314000756/https://sloan.org/past-fellows|url-status=dead}}</ref> becoming the first black recipient of this fellowship. In 1997 she also was awarded a [[Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers: Recipient Details {{!}} NSF - National Science Foundation |url=https://www.nsf.gov/awards/PECASE/recip_details.jsp;jsessionid=400B97FD272755584154FC2C07DAE15D?pecase_id=32 |access-date=2022-08-11 |website=www.nsf.gov}}</ref> for both her mathematical research and her development of mathematics curricula for inner-city school children. This award is given to only 60 scientists and engineers each year and has a prize of $500,000.<ref name=Spangenburg/> In 2009, she presented the [[AWM/MAA Falconer Lecture|Etta Z. Falconer Lecture]] on "The Sum of Squares of Wavelengths of a Closed Surface"<ref>{{Cite web |title=Falconer Lectures |url=https://awm-math.org/awards/falconer-lectures/ |access-date=2026-04-10 |website=Association for Women in Mathematics (AWM) |language=en-US}}</ref> an award given by the [[Association for Women in Mathematics|AWM]] for women with distinguished careers in mathematics or mathematics education.
